headline: Provable circuit-level thresholds for non-abelian topological phases
text: We provide an explicit scheme to realize a quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological order. For this, we construct syndrome extraction circuits based on the Turaev-Viro path integral as well as a classical algorithm for decoding on the fly. We prove that our scheme has a threshold under a local stochastic circuit-level noise model and discuss how to generalize it to implement topological logical gates.

headline: Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems
text: Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. text: Learning dexterous manipulation from limited visual demonstrations is challenging because policies must acquire both perceptual grounding and precise control, while reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can acquire rich control behaviors from large-scale interaction with privileged information. text: Infleqtion 30 Logical Qubits Rely on Error Detection Table of Contents September 24, 2026 – Infleqtion (NYSE: INFQ) said it had entangled 30 logical qubits encoded in 80 atoms on its Sqale neutral-atom quantum computer, meeting the logical-qubit target it had set for 2026. The company announced the result at Quantum World Congress 2026 and said the experiments were completed in August. Infleqtion builds neutral-atom quantum computers, optical clocks and quantum sensors. Its shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange in February after it completed a business combination with Churchill Capital Corp X. The company said the new result made it the first neutral-atom quantum computing company to reach 30 logical qubits on a commercial system. Each block was prepared in the logical zero state of the distance-3 [[8,3,3]] code and then operated in the distance-2 [[8,3,2]] code, which Infleqtion said can detect any error or correct for a lost atom. Each block encodes three logical qubits. The test was an instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) circuit whose entangling gates, four logical controlled-controlled-Z (CCZ) gates among them, connected all 30 logical qubits. Infleqtion said the circuit placed all 30 in a single coherent state. The company said the circuit used 136 physical two-qubit gates and about 1,000 physical operations in total, an amount it called one KiloQuOp. Of the more than one billion possible 30-bit outputs, the ideal circuit produces 262,144, or one in 4,096. Infleqtion reported that about 25% of its measured outputs fell inside that set, roughly 1,000 times the rate that uniformly random outputs would achieve. text: NATO Opens Counter-Drone Marketplace With 16 Systems From Five Companies - Inside Unmanned Systems On Nov. 5, NATO launched a Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems (C-UAS) marketplace. Allies can buy pre-selected counter-drone solutions directly from a NATO catalog, with no further tender required. Image: NATO The NATO Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) competed and selected 16 solutions from five companies: Alta Ares, Axon Enterprise, Northrop Grumman, OSL UK and Quantum Systems. NATO said the selected capabilities have already been deployed in allied countries and in Ukraine. They include static, transportable and on-the-move systems. The marketplace is part of Drone Edge, an initiative launched at the NATO Summit Defence Industry Forum in Ankara in July. Under Drone Edge, allies committed to investing more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over the next five years. NATO has also allocated €3.1 million to fund further testing of the selected systems by nations or NATO commands. Four Reference Scenarios NCIA evaluated bids against four reference scenarios. Area protection covers a zone up to 3 kilometers in diameter, such as an airbase or logistics hub. Border protection extends across a 20-kilometer border segment. Convoy protection covers a moving column up to 300 meters long traveling at up to 50 kilometers per hour. Point protection focuses on a single high-value asset or location, such as a command post. NCIA hosts the NATO Counter-UAS Centre of Expertise and manages the multi-award framework contracts, which are valid for 18 months. NATO intends to run regular competitions so that newer technologies reach allies. The frameworks are not purchase orders in themselves. Individual orders will be placed through subsequent contracts with the selected suppliers. The competition predates Drone Edge. Generation III+ Small Modular Reactor Program Background U.S. electricity demand is forecast to soar in the coming years driven by consumer needs, data center growth, increased AI use, and the industrial sector’s need for constant power. Small modular reactors could provide reliable power for these energy-intensive sectors, with the added benefit of flexible deployment thanks to their compact size and modular design. The chemical company has launched its Faizeon dielectric fluids, which it hopes will give data center operators “highly efficient options that can support evolving system architectures and remove heat from high-power processors and servers.” – Chemours While most data centers using liquid cooling currently rely on single-phase direct-to-chip solutions, it is widely anticipated that a switch to two-phase, where server heat is absorbed by liquid, then vaporized, will be needed for future generations of powerful AI accelerators. Chemours said its Faizeon 200 fluid maintained a GPU at up to 19°C (66°F) lower than a single-phase, water-based fluid, while using a lower coolant flow rate. "AI's rapid growth is increasing the demands on data center infrastructure, and cooling is becoming a critical constraint," said Denise Dignam, president and CEO at Chemours. "With our liquid cooling solutions, we are applying more than 90 years of thermal management expertise to help data centers manage higher heat loads while improving performance and dramatically reducing energy and water demand. “Our Faizeon liquid cooling team is collaborating across the data center ecosystem to bring together the expertise, testing, and support needed to confidently deploy two-phase liquid cooling at scale." Chemours said it has worked with the US Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), NTT DATA, 2CRSi, DataVolt, Munters, Accelsius, and ZutaCore on the development of the fluid. The six year old company says it is one of the few suppliers globally supplying full voltage range GaN product coverage, and currently the only GaN designer who can provide mass production GaN product for customer validation in Taiwan. The company says it can provide GaN device solutions tailored to different power topologies from low-mid voltage DC-DC/DC-AC conversion to high voltage AC-DC/DC-DC conversion. headline: Five companies (incl. Axon, Northrop Grumman) join NATO's C-UAS marketplace; 16 systems selected for direct ally procurement
text: Five companies join NATO’s new C-UAS marketplace - Unmanned airspace Skip to content NATO’s Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) announced on 5 November that it has selected 16 systems from five companies for the NATO counter-uncrewed aerial systems (C-UAS) marketplace. The marketplace, which NCIA manages, was first announced in July. It is part of NATO’s Drone Edge, which is investing over USD 40 billion in C-UAS capabilities over the next five years. Through the marketplace, Allies can procure directly from the NATO catalogue without any further tender process. The five selected companies announced yesterday are Alta Ares, Axon Enterprise Inc., Northrop Grumman, OSL UK and Quantum Systems. The selected equipment covers a mix of static, transportable and on-the-move systems. Each company has already deployed systems in Allied countries and in Ukraine. NCIA selected the capabilities based on the following four reference scenarios: The Point Protection scenario focuses on enhancing the protection of a specific high-value asset or location – such as a military installation, critical infrastructure or command post – through effective detection, tracking and response. The Area Protection scenario focuses on the protection of a larger geographical area up to 3km in diameter, such as an airbase, logistics hub or military installation, through coordinated sensors and countermeasures against drone threats. The Border Protection scenario extends monitoring and protection across a 20 km border segment through persistent surveillance, early detection, tracking and coordinated responses. The Convoy Protection scenario focuses on the protection of moving military convoy up to 300-meter length, travelling at speeds of up to 50 km/h, through mobile C-UAS capabilities capable of detecting, tracking and responding to threats while on the move. By the PubCo Insight Editorial Team , edited by Brad Listermann · November 7, 2026 Regulatory hurdles, not tech, slow autonomous security robot adoption. On November 6th and 7th, Axon Enterprise (AXON) reported a significant revenue miss and cut its guidance, sending its stock plunging. The company attributed this directly to federal delays impacting drone deals. This is not just an Axon problem. These delays are slowing the deployment of autonomous security robots and drone-based first responder initiatives across the board. The bottleneck is real, and it affects every operator in this space. The Mechanism of Federal Delay Autonomous security robots and drone-based systems, especially those intended for public safety or critical infrastructure, often operate under a patchwork of federal, state, and local regulations. The core issue lies in the permitting and approval process for expanded operational envelopes. Current FAA regulations, for example, typically require line-of-sight operation for drones. Waivers for beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) operations are complex, time-consuming, and often granted on a case-by-case basis, limiting scalability. For ground-based robots, state and municipal ordinances around public right-of-way and liability create similar hurdles. headline: What is immersion cooling for data centers? - Vertiv
text: What is immersion cooling for data centers? null Home Insights What is immersion cooling for data centers? What is immersion cooling for data centers? 8 min. Read 11/6/26 Rising AI rack densities are pushing traditional cooling approaches further. Immersion cooling brings liquid directly to IT equipment to manage higher heat loads. Immersion cooling for data centers is a liquid cooling method that replaces traditional IT equipment racks with sealed tanks or enclosures filled with thermally conductive dielectric fluid. Servers and other components are submerged in the fluid, which absorbs heat directly from hardware surfaces and transfers it away from the IT equipment. Data centers supporting AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads are key use cases for immersion cooling as rack densities increase. Immersion cooling can support higher heat loads and help reduce fan and facility energy use, but it can require significant equipment and operational changes within the data center. How immersion cooling works Immersion cooling submerges IT equipment in dielectric fluid, allowing the fluid to absorb heat directly from the components. The system then transfers that heat away from the IT equipment and ultimately to the facility cooling infrastructure. The way the fluid transfers and rejects heat depends on the type of immersion cooling system. The two primary approaches are single-phase and two-phase immersion cooling. Single-phase immersion cooling Immersion cooling involves placing IT equipment horizontally in a sealed tank that resembles a server rack on its back. Servers are inserted from the top and position them vertically in dielectric fluid. The fluid absorbs heat directly from the submerged IT components, reducing the number of heat-transfer steps compared with air cooling. (see Figure 1) Figure 1. text: Omen AI Acquires Aquatic Labs For $16 Million To Expand Data Center Cooling Technology × Search Pulse 2.0 Omen AI Acquires Aquatic Labs For $16 Million To Expand Data Center Cooling Technology Omen AI, a San Francisco-based company developing automated fluid-monitoring technology for artificial intelligence data centers, has acquired Aquatic Labs for $16 million in cash and stock. The acquisition brings Aquatic Labs’ sensing technology and research team into Omen AI as it expands its capabilities for monitoring and maintaining data center cooling systems. Aquatic Labs founder Allan Adams will become Omen AI’s chief science officer and lead research and development activities. Adams previously worked as a physics professor at MIT and as a visiting oceanographer at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. Omen AI develops sensors designed to analyze cooling fluids continuously while data center equipment is operating. Traditional testing often requires operators to collect fluid samples and send them to laboratories for analysis. Omen AI aims to bring those measurements directly into cooling infrastructure, allowing operators to identify changes in fluid chemistry and biological conditions before they cause operational problems. Aquatic Labs contributes technology that measures total alkalinity in real time without requiring chemicals to be added during each test. This capability can help operators evaluate conditions associated with corrosion and mineral deposits inside cooling systems. The technology will complement Omen AI’s existing elemental analysis and biological monitoring capabilities. The company expects to begin shipping products incorporating the additional monitoring technologies by the end of 2026. Its longer-term goal is to develop cooling systems capable of automatically adjusting fluid chemistry within approved operating limits and verifying the results through continued measurement. The collaboration aligns Fourier’s liquid‑cooled modular data center platforms with UNICOM Engineering’s liquid‑cooled portfolio built on Tier-1 platforms, supported by integration, supply chain execution, and deployment expertise to help customers move faster from power availability to operational AI capacity at scale. Fourier delivers prefabricated, containerized infrastructure engineered for high‑density AI workloads, enabling liquid cooling architectures such as direct‑to‑chip, immersion, and hybrid fan‑wall designs. These platforms are designed for repeatable deployments and standardized expansion as GPU densities increase. UNICOM Engineering enables these platforms through full ITE delivery, including integration, deployment, lifecycle services, inventory and logistics programs, and enterprise-grade warranty support. Fourier reports more than 600 megawatts of deployed and in‑progress liquid‑cooled infrastructure, reflecting growing global demand for modular, cooling‑first AI data center design. headline: Fortem Technologies selected as prime contractor for USD1 billion DHS counter-drone IDIQ contract
text: Fortem Technologies selected as prime contractor for USD1 billion DHS counter-drone IDIQ contract - Unmanned airspace Skip to content Fortem Technologies has been selected as a prime contractor for the US Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) five-year Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems (C-UAS) indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contract, the company said in a press release. Fortem reports it is the only small business among the seven companies selected under the contract’s Track 1 – Hardware/Software and Ancillary Services, which has an estimated starting ceiling value of USD 1.011 billion. The award enables DHS components, including US Customs and Border Protection, the Secret Service, the Federal Protective Service and the US Coast Guard, to place task orders directly with the company for its counter-drone technologies. Fortem said its subcontracting team includes Lockheed Martin and Microsoft, providing additional electro-optical/infrared, radio frequency, passive radar and C4 capabilities through the contract vehicle.
